Do not misunderstand me: I was never truly mad. Even when my frantic thoughts seemed to be driving me into insanity, I remained aware of my condition, and I revealed those thoughts only to silence and solitude. The people around me knew nothing of it. They saw only a poor girl with a broken spirit, speaking in a soft, quiet voice, beneath whose lowered eyelids tears sometimes slipped out, which she tried to conceal. Someone who preferred to be alone and recoiled from attention; someone who never smiled—oh, no, I never smiled—and that was all.

Well, I escaped. I left my guardian’s house and was never heard from again. The letters I left behind, and other circumstances I deliberately arranged, led people to believe I had killed myself. They therefore searched less carefully than they otherwise would have, and before long every trace and memory of me disappeared. I left London aboard a small vessel heading for a port in northern England. Now that my attempt had succeeded and I was entirely alone, peace returned. The sea was calm and the vessel glided gently forward. Sitting on deck beneath the open sky, I felt as though I had become a different person. I was no longer the wild, raving, desperately unhappy Mathilda, but a young female hermit devoted to seclusion, who must strive to keep her heart free of turmoil and unholy despair. The fanciful, nunlike clothing I had adopted; the knowledge that my very existence was a secret known only to me; the solitude destined to fill the rest of my life—all nurtured gentle thoughts in my wounded heart. The breeze moving through my hair revived me. With peaceful eyes I watched sunlight glitter on the waves, and birds chase one another across the water, just brushing it with their feathers. I also slept without disturbing dreams and woke refreshed, ready to enjoy my quiet freedom once again.

Four days later we reached our destination harbour. I would not stay on the coast, but immediately travelled inland. I had already decided what sort of place I would live in: an isolated house on a broad plain, far from any other dwelling, where I could see the entire horizon and wander great distances without being troubled by the sight of other people. I did not hate humanity, but felt that the calm flow of my emotions depended on being alone. I settled in a wide, solitary place, on a bleak heath scattered with stones, short grass growing between them, and here and there a few rushes beside a small pool.

For a moment I was too astonished to think clearly. I knew my drawing differed greatly from this one in its details, though their general outlines were somewhat alike. Then I took a candle, sat down at the other end of the room, and examined the parchment more closely. When I turned it over, I found my own sketch on the back, exactly as I had drawn it. At first I was simply amazed by the remarkable likeness of the outlines. What an extraordinary coincidence: without my knowing it, a skull had been drawn on the other side of the parchment, directly behind my picture of the beetle. And that skull resembled my drawing not only in shape but also in size. The strangeness of this coincidence left me quite stunned for a while. Such coincidences usually have that effect. The mind tries to establish a connection, a chain of cause and effect, and when it cannot, it becomes briefly unable to function. But as I recovered from my bewilderment, I slowly became certain of something that startled me even more than the coincidence itself. I began to remember clearly, beyond any doubt, that there had been no drawing on the parchment when I sketched the beetle. I grew completely sure, because I remembered examining both sides, one after the other, to find the cleanest place to draw. If the skull had been there then, I could not possibly have missed it. Here was a mystery I felt unable to explain. Yet even at that early stage, in the deepest, most hidden corner of my mind, the faintest idea began to glow like a tiny luminous insect: an idea of the truth that last night’s adventure proved so magnificently. I got up immediately, put the parchment safely away, and decided to think no more about it until I was alone.

We had discovered the beetle on the mainland coast, about a mile east of the island and only a short distance above the high-water line. When I picked it up, it bit me sharply and made me drop it. The insect flew towards Jupiter. With his usual caution, before trying to catch it he looked around for a leaf, or something similar, to protect his hand while he held it.

Their arrival had kindled a sort of fire in Saint Antoine’s heart, spreading rapidly as they passed, flaring and flickering in the faces at nearly every doorway and window. Yet nobody had followed them, and when they entered the wine shop no one spoke, although every man inside turned his eyes toward them.

“Good day, gentlemen!” said Monsieur Defarge.

Perhaps this was the signal that allowed everyone to speak. It brought a chorus of “Good day!” in reply.

“The weather is bad, gentlemen,” Defarge said, shaking his head.

At this, each man glanced at his neighbour, and then they all lowered their eyes and sat in silence. All except one, who stood up and left.

“My wife,” Defarge said aloud to Madame Defarge, “I have travelled several leagues with this good road mender, whose name is Jacques. I met him—by chance—a day and a half’s journey outside Paris. He’s a good lad, this road mender called Jacques. Give him something to drink, my wife!”

A second man rose and went out. Madame Defarge placed wine before the road mender called Jacques, who removed his blue cap in greeting to the company and drank. He had some coarse, dark bread tucked into the front of his blouse. Sitting near Madame Defarge’s counter, he chewed pieces of it between drinks. A third man got up and left.

Defarge refreshed himself with a glass of wine, though he took less than the stranger had been given, since wine was no rare treat for him. He stood waiting while the countryman ate his breakfast. He looked at nobody in the room, and nobody now looked at him—not even Madame Defarge, who had picked up her knitting and was busy with it.

“Have you finished your meal, my friend?” he asked when the time seemed right.

“Yes, thank you.”

“Then come along! I’ll show you the room I said you could stay in. It will suit you perfectly.”

Out of the wine shop and into the street, from the street into a courtyard, from the courtyard up a steep staircase, and from the staircase into an attic—the same attic where a white-haired man had once sat on a low bench, bent forward and absorbed in making shoes.

There was no white-haired man there now. Instead there were the three men who had left the wine shop separately. One small connection joined them to the white-haired man now far away: they had once peered at him through cracks in the wall.

Defarge carefully shut the door and spoke quietly.

“Jacques One, Jacques Two, Jacques Three! This is the witness whom I, Jacques Four, met by arrangement.
